links.why: Zeeman splitting $\mp\frac12g\mu_B\mu_0H$ of a spin-$\frac12$, the spin-$S$ sum giving $S(S+1)$, and the singlet/triplet spectrum of two spins (QM sheets 11-14).
Zeeman splitting and 21 cm hyperfine line (spin flips) are the astronomical use of the same spin physics.

intro: The vault holds spins. A metal answers a field weakly (Pauli), localised moments answer strongly (Curie), and exchange turns paramagnets into ferro- or antiferromagnets. Compute Weiss temperatures and the field that tips a Néel state to saturation, and watch the sign conventions.

encounters.title: Para- and diamagnetism: Curie, Pauli, Landau

blocks.html: Free spins align against thermal disorder: $\chi\propto1/T$. In a metal only the $\nu(\epsilon_F)k_BT$ electrons at the Fermi surface can flip, each giving $\propto1/k_BT$: the temperatures cancel, $\chi_P$ is constant and $\sim T/T_F$ times the Curie value. Orbital motion gives Landau diamagnetism, one third of $\chi_P$ for free electrons.
Stoner: an on-site repulsion $U$ acts like an extra field $\propto M$; $\chi=\chi_P/(1-\frac{2UV_0}{\mu_0(g\mu_B)^2}\chi_P)$ diverges when $U\nu$ is large: band ferromagnetism (Fe, Co, Ni).
Pauli paramagnetism is $T$-independent; a Curie tail in a metal signals magnetic impurities. Cu is overall diamagnetic (core electrons and $(m_e/m^*)^2$).

blocks.html: Exchange is Coulomb repulsion plus Pauli: two spins in an orbital-overlap region feel a spin-dependent energy far larger (tens of meV) than their dipolar coupling (0.1 meV). In mean field each spin sees the average of its neighbours as an extra 'Weiss field', which turns $C/T$ into $C/(T-T_W)$.

Sign conventions differ. Zheludev's exams: $H=+\sum J\vec S\cdot\vec S$ ($J<0$ ferro) and $T_W=-J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/3k_B$. Both printed keys give saturation fields twice $2J_{\rm AF}S/g\mu_B\mu_0$ because they count each bond twice in the energy per spin; the exact two-spin check ($g\mu_B\mu_0H=J$) supports the formula above. State your convention and keep it.

Jan 2024: brick-wall 'honeycomb' lattice, one $J_1$ and two $J_2$ bonds per site, $J_{\rm total}=J_1+2J_2$. Aug 2024: triangular lattice, two $J_1$ and four $J_2$, $J_{\rm total}=2J_1+4J_2$. Both ask: ground state sketch, $T_W$, saturation field.

encounters.title: Curie–Weiss law from the Weiss field
encounters.goal: Starting from the Heisenberg model and the free-spin Curie law $M=\chi_SH$ with $\chi_S=C/T$, derive $\chi=C/(T-T_W)$ and $k_BT_W=J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/3$.
given: $\vec S_i=\langle\vec S\rangle+\delta\vec S_i$; drop $\delta\vec S_i\cdot\delta\vec S_j$

steps.reveal: $H_i^{MF}=-J_{\rm total}\vec S_i\cdot\langle\vec S\rangle=-\frac{J_{\rm total}V_0}{g\mu_B}\vec S_i\cdot\vec M$.

steps.prompt: Compare with Zeeman $-g\mu_B\mu_0\vec S\cdot\vec H$: effective field.

steps.reveal: $T_W=J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/3k_B$. Brick-wall lattice: $J_{\rm total}=J_1+2J_2$; triangular: $2J_1+4J_2$. Exact at high $T$: the best way to measure $J$.

keyPoints: sum $J$ over all neighbours of one spin

encounters.title: Why a metal is only weakly magnetic: Pauli versus Curie
encounters.problem: Script 6.2: sodium, $n=2.65\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ (one electron per atom), $g=2$. Free electron gas: $\epsilon_F=\hbar^2(3\pi^2n)^{2/3}/2m$, $\nu(\epsilon_F)=3n/2\epsilon_F$. Pauli susceptibility $\chi_P=\mu_0\frac{(g\mu_B)^2}{4}\nu(\epsilon_F)$. For comparison, the same number of **localised** $S=\frac12$ moments would obey Curie, $\chi=C/T$ with $C=\mu_0\frac{(g\mu_B)^2S(S+1)}{3k_BV_0}$, $V_0=1/n$. Room temperature $T=300$ K.

steps.prompt: Density of states at the Fermi energy $\nu(\epsilon_F)=3n/(2\epsilon_F)$ in J$^{-1}$m$^{-3}$.
steps.hint: Both spin directions included. Each spin species has $\nu/2$.

Only the electrons in a shell $\sim\nu k_BT$ at $\epsilon_F$ can flip their spin, each contributing $\propto1/k_BT$: the $T$ cancels (script 6.12-6.16). $\chi_P\approx8\times10^{-6}$: weak, positive, temperature independent.

steps.prompt: Curie susceptibility the same number of free $S=\frac12$ moments would have at 300 K, $\mu_0(g\mu_B)^2n/(4k_BT)$.

steps.hint: Exactly $2\epsilon_F/(3k_BT)\approx83$: the Pauli principle suppresses the susceptibility by $T/T_F$. Landau diamagnetism adds $\chi_L=-\chi_P/3$ (script 6.17), so a free-electron metal is still paramagnetic.

encounters.title: Weiss temperature on a lattice with two couplings
encounters.problem: Zheludev, Jan 2024, Problem 4 / Aug 2024, Problem 4, with numbers. **Convention of this script (6.63):** $H=-\sum_{\{i,j\}}J_{ij}\,\vec S_i\cdot\vec S_j$ over each bond once, so $J>0$ is ferromagnetic and $k_BT_W=J_{\rm total}\,S(S+1)/3$ with $J_{\rm total}=\sum_jJ_{ij}$ over all neighbours of one spin (6.60-6.65). The exam sheets use the opposite sign ($H=+\sum J\,\vec S\cdot\vec S$, $J>0$ antiferromagnetic) and write $T_W=-J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/3k_B$; **always read the sign convention off the problem.** Spins $S=1$. The brick-wall (honeycomb) lattice has per site one ferromagnetic $J_1=+2.0$ meV bond and two antiferromagnetic $J_2=-1.5$ meV bonds. The triangular lattice has per site two $J_1$ and four $J_2$ bonds.

steps.prompt: $J_{\rm total}=J_1+2J_2$ for the honeycomb lattice, in meV.
steps.hint: Sum over all neighbours of one spin: one $J_1$ bond and two $J_2$ bonds. Negative: net antiferromagnetic.

steps.prompt: Weiss temperature $T_W=J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/(3k_B)$ in K (keep the sign).
steps.hint: $-1.0\,{\rm meV}\times2/3=-0.67$ meV $=-7.7$ K. The Curie–Weiss law $\chi=C/(T-T_W)$ extrapolates to a negative intercept: antiferromagnetic correlations although the $J_1$ dimers are ferromagnetic.

steps.prompt: Triangular lattice with the same $J_1,J_2$: $T_W$ in K.
steps.hint: $J_{\rm total}=2J_1+4J_2=-2$ meV, exactly twice the honeycomb result because there are twice as many neighbours with the same ratio $J_1:J_2$.

steps.prompt: Curie–Weiss at $T=50$ K: susceptibility relative to non-interacting spins, $\chi/\chi_0=T/(T-T_W)$.
steps.hint: $\chi=C/(T-T_W)$ with $T_W<0$ lowers $\chi$ below the free-spin Curie value $C/T$ (antiferromagnetic correlations). A ferromagnet ($T_W>0$) would enhance it and diverge at $T_W$. In the ordered state the ground state here is an antiferromagnet of ferromagnetic dimers: the Néel arrangement of dimers satisfies every bond (any common rotation of all spins is also a ground state).

encounters.title: At what field is the antiferromagnet saturated?
encounters.problem: Same lattices, $S=1$, $g=2$, $J_2=-1.5$ meV (antiferromagnetic in this script's sign convention; $|J_2|=1.5$ meV). Apply a field $\mu_0H\perp$ the Néel axis at $T=0$. In the canted state the sublattice spins tilt by an angle $\theta$ towards the field; the energy per spin is $E(\theta)=\text{const}-\tfrac12J_{\rm AF}S^2\cos2\theta-g\mu_B\mu_0HS\sin\theta$, where $J_{\rm AF}=\sum|J|$ runs over the antiferromagnetic neighbours of one spin (each bond is shared by two spins, hence the $\frac12$) and the ferromagnetic bonds are unaffected by the canting. Minimising gives $g\mu_B\mu_0H=2J_{\rm AF}S\sin\theta$, saturation at $\theta=\pi/2$.

steps.prompt: $J_{\rm AF}$ for the honeycomb lattice (two antiferromagnetic $J_2$ neighbours per spin), in meV.
Saturation field $\mu_0H_{\rm sat}=2J_{\rm AF}S/(g\mu_B)$ for the honeycomb lattice in tesla.
steps.hint: $2\times3.0\,{\rm meV}\times1/(2\times0.0579\,{\rm meV/T})=51.8$ T. Check from the script: $H=2\frac{J_{\rm total}}{(g\mu_B)^2\mu_0}2V_0|M_1|\sin\alpha$ with $|M_1|=g\mu_BS/2V_0$ (6.73-6.78): same. **The printed exam keys give twice this** ($8J_2S/g\mu_B\mu_0$ for honeycomb, $16J_2S$ for the triangular lattice): they count every bond fully in the energy per spin (ordered pairs) while their $T_W$ counts each bond once; with the script's convention the factor is as above. Test: two $S=\frac12$ spins with one bond $J$: singlet and $m=1$ triplet cross at $g\mu_B\mu_0H=J$, which the formula reproduces ($2\cdot1\cdot J\cdot\frac12$).

steps.prompt: Triangular lattice (four antiferromagnetic $J_2$ neighbours): saturation field in tesla.
steps.hint: $J_{\rm AF}=4|J_2|=6$ meV: twice the honeycomb value. The $J_1$ rows stay ferromagnetic throughout.

steps.prompt: Check on the quantum limit: two spins $S=\frac12$, one bond $|J|=1$ meV, $g=2$. Field at which the singlet–triplet crossing happens, in tesla.
steps.hint: Crossing at $g\mu_B\mu_0H=|J|$: $8.64$ T. This is exactly $2ZJS/g\mu_B$ with $Z=1,S=\frac12$, and it fixes the factor of 2 beyond doubt.

encounters.title: Exchange versus dipoles: how strong is iron's exchange?
encounters.problem: Quick fight. Iron is ferromagnetic up to $T_C=1043$ K (bcc, $Z=8$ nearest neighbours, take $S=1$). Mean field: $k_BT_C=|J|Z\,S(S+1)/3$ (script 6.72). Script 6.2.5: the magnetic dipolar interaction between neighbouring electrons is only $\sim0.1$ meV ($\sim1$ K). Estimate $|J|$ in meV (within a factor of 1.3) and compare.

steps.hint: $3\times0.0862\,{\rm meV/K}\times1043/(8\times2)=16.9$ meV. Mean field overestimates $T_C$ a little, so the true $J$ is somewhat larger.

steps.prompt: How many times stronger than the dipolar energy is it, $|J|/E_{\rm dip}$?
steps.hint: A factor $\sim170$: dipoles would give $T_C\sim6$ K, not 1043 K. The effective spin–spin interaction comes from Coulomb repulsion plus the Pauli principle (script 6.3.1), not from magnetism at all.

encounters.title: Boss: magnetism on a triangular lattice (exam problem)

source.where: Problem 4 'Magnetism' (Zheludev, 16 Aug 2024); solution: solutions/Einführung in die Festkörperphysik HS23 (Solution).pdf, Problem 4

encounters.instructions: Statement and signs are the exam's: **here $J>0$ is antiferromagnetic** ($H=+\sum J\vec S_i\cdot\vec S_j$). Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the game numbers. Pay attention to the factor in (f): compare with your own derivation.
statement: Consider the following lattice of magnetic atoms of spin $S$ (a triangular lattice, drawn with horizontal rows). The magnetic atoms are coupled by Heisenberg couplings $J_1\ne J_2$: $J_1$ (solid line) along the rows, $J_2$ (dashed) along the two diagonals. Each spin has 2 neighbours at $J_1$ and 4 at $J_2$. First both couplings are ferromagnetic, $J_1,J_2<0$.
(a) [0.5 pt] Draw a ground-state spin configuration.  (b) [0.5 pt] Is there another ground state? If so, draw it.  (c) [0.5 pt] Find the Weiss temperature.
Now for the same lattice $J_1<0$ and $J_2>0$.

(d) [0.5 pt] Draw a ground-state spin configuration.  (e) [0.5 pt] Find the Weiss temperature.  (f) [0.5 pt] A field $H\perp\vec S$ is applied perpendicular to the spin direction of (d). At what magnitude of $H$ is the moment saturated? Assume $T=0$.

finalAnswers.prompt: (c) Weiss temperature in K, $T_W=-(2J_1+4J_2)S(S+1)/3k_B$ with $J_1=-0.40$, $J_2=-0.20$ meV.
(e) Weiss temperature in K for $J_1=-0.40$, $J_2=+0.50$ meV (keep the sign).
(d) Classical ground-state energy per spin in meV: $J_1S^2-2J_2S^2$ for the ferromagnetic rows, antiparallel between rows.
(f) Saturation field $\mu_0H_{\rm sat}=2\cdot(4J_2)S/(g\mu_B)$ in tesla (derive it; compare with the printed key).

keyPoints: (a) Ferromagnetic ground state: all spins parallel (any common direction; all bonds satisfied).
(b) Any rotation of the common direction; no other (collinear) state with all bonds satisfied.

(c) $T_W=-\sum_{\rm neighbours}J\,\dfrac{S(S+1)}{3k_B}=-(2J_1+4J_2)\dfrac{S(S+1)}{3k_B}$ (exam sign convention $H=+J\vec S\cdot\vec S$; the script's $-J$ convention gives $+J_{\rm total}S(S+1)/3k_B$). Positive for $J_1,J_2<0$.
(d) Ferromagnetic rows ($J_1<0$), antiparallel between neighbouring rows ($J_2>0$): each spin has two neighbours in the row above and two below, all antiparallel, so all bonds are satisfied.

(f) Canted energy per spin: $E(\theta)=J_1S^2-2J_2S^2\cos2\theta-g\mu_B\mu_0HS\sin\theta$ (each of the 4 antiferromagnetic bonds counted with weight $\frac12$). $\partial E/\partial\theta=0$: $8J_2S\sin\theta=g\mu_B\mu_0H$; saturated at $\theta=\pi/2$: $\mu_0H_{\rm sat}=8J_2S/(g\mu_B)$. The printed key writes $E=2J_1S^2+4J_2S^2\cos(\pi-2\theta)-\ldots$ (every bond with weight 1) and finds $16J_2S/(g\mu_B\mu_0)$; with the same bond convention as its $T_W$ (each bond once) the result is $8J_2S/(g\mu_B\mu_0)$, confirmed by the two-spin singlet–triplet check $g\mu_B\mu_0H=J$. State your convention in the exam and keep it consistent between (c)/(e) and (f).

(f) Alternative route (script 6.78): $H=2\frac{J_{\rm total}}{(g\mu_B)^2\mu_0}2V_0|M_1|\sin\alpha$ with $J_{\rm total}\to4J_2$ and $|M_1|=g\mu_BS/2V_0$ (the sublattice magnetisation is normalised to the full volume, script 6.73).
